title: Real projects and tests
summary: Modules, the Cargo layout, the commands you type daily, and tests that run.

blocks.html: Everything so far has been one file. A real project is a folder Cargo manages. Cargo.toml is its manifest: name, version, and edition — 2021 for everything in this book. The src/ folder holds the code. src/main.rs is the binary's entry point, and src/lib.rs is the library that other files hang off. A project may have both, and most real ones do: the binary stays thin and the logic lives in the library where tests can reach it.

blocks.title: what a Cargo project looks like
blocks.ascii:
myapp/
  Cargo.toml        name, version, edition
  src/
    main.rs         fn main: the binary
    lib.rs          the library
    parser.rs       one module of the library
  tests/
    parser.rs       integration tests
  target/           build output (never edit)

blocks.html: Inside a file, mod name { ... } starts a module: a block with its own namespace. Everything in it is private until you write pub, and private means parent code cannot reach it at all — not "should not", cannot. That is how Rust keeps an implementation detail from quietly becoming somebody else's dependency.

blocks.title: a module with a private helper

blocks.html: Paths name items. crate:: starts from this crate's root, super:: means the parent module, self:: the current one. use writes a path once and then the short name works — it is an alias, not an include, so an unused use is a warning, not dead weight. Modules nest, and each level keeps its own privacy:

blocks.title: nested modules, use, and super

blocks.html: The commands you will type every day. cargo run builds and runs. cargo build --release builds an optimized binary into target/release/. cargo check type-checks without writing a binary — the one to run in a loop while thinking. cargo test builds and runs every test. cargo doc --open builds documentation for your crate and its dependencies and opens it. rustup doc opens the offline bookshelf this course links into.

A test is a function marked #[test], normally collected in a #[cfg(test)] mod tests at the bottom of the file it tests; cfg(test) means the module is compiled only for tests, so it costs nothing in a release build. assert_eq!(a, b) checks that two values are equal, assert!(cond) checks one condition, and #[should_panic] marks a test that is supposed to panic — useful when panicking is the documented behavior. Files in tests/ are integration tests: they use your crate the way a user would.

blocks.title: tests that run
blocks.output:
running 3 tests
test tests::adds_a_negative_number ... ok
test tests::adds_two_numbers ... ok
test tests::dividing_by_zero_panics - should panic ... ok
test result: ok. 3 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 0 filtered out

blocks.html:
That is the shape of a real project: a manifest, modules with a deliberate public surface, and tests next to the code they cover. You have now seen all of it — values, ownership, the types you build, collections, failure, traits, and a project that compiles.

What next depends on what you are writing. The Book is the long-form version of this course: read it from chapter 12 onward and it takes the detours we skipped — a real I/O project, smart pointers, concurrency, patterns. If you would rather read programs than prose, Rust by Example has every idea above as a runnable file. And keep rustup doc one keystroke away: it opens the same bookshelf offline, and the standard library page has a search box that answers "what is this method called" faster than any search engine.

quiz.q: An item sits inside mod parse with no pub in front of it. Who can use it?
options: Code in that module and in modules nested inside it
Any other crate that depends on this one
quiz.why: Privacy is the default and it flows inward: the module and its children can see the item, the parent cannot. pub is what opens it up one level at a time.

quiz.q: Which command type-checks the project and reports errors without producing a binary?
quiz.why: cargo check stops after analysis, so it is much faster than a build. That is why it is the command people keep running while they think.

quiz.q: Where does a file belong so that it is an integration test rather than a unit test?
options: In the tests/ folder at the top of the project
In src/, next to the code it tests
Anywhere, as long as it ends in .rs
quiz.why: Files in tests/ are compiled as their own crates that link your library and call it like an external user would. Unit tests live inside src/ behind #[cfg(test)].

exercise.brief: Add a public triple function to the math module that returns n times 3 — then uncomment the last line in main so the program prints it.
exercise.hint: Inside the module, write pub fn triple(n: i32) -> i32 { n * 3 }. Without pub, main cannot see it: private items are invisible to the code outside their module.
